extracted_content.title: Overview
extracted_content.content: Section 1833(q) of the Social Security Act requires charges for some Medicare Program services to be submitted with ordering or referring provider information from a qualified healthcare provider. This requirement ensures quality of care because many services require a qualified healthcare provider to interpret and provide guidance to the patient. Supplying a valid National Provider Identifier (NPI) of the ordering or referring qualified healthcare provider helps in the verification that services rendered were necessary and medically reviewed and that follow-up care is available. Original Medicare began rejecting claims without valid ordering or referring provider information January 6, 2014.

extracted_content.title: Valid Order or Referral Requirement
extracted_content.hierarchy_path: Medicare Advantage Payment Policy > Valid Order or Referral Requirement
extracted_content.content: Humana plans require valid orders for the same types of services for which Original Medicare requires orders and require valid referrals for the same types of services for which Original Medicare requires referrals. To be valid, an order or referral must have been issued by a qualified healthcare provider. The services of a Part A home health agency, specifically, may only be ordered or referred by a doctor of medicine, doctor of osteopathy or doctor of podiatry. Humana plans deny charges for services for which Humana requires valid orders or referrals when those services were provided in the absence of an applicable, valid order or referral; when appropriate, plans require reimbursement of overpayments.

extracted_content.title: Order or Referral Documentation
extracted_content.hierarchy_path: Medicare Advantage Payment Policy > Order or Referral Documentation
extracted_content.content: Humana requires providers to maintain complete and accurate documentation of orders and referrals for services for which Humana requires orders and referrals. Humana requires providers to make order and referral documentation available to Humana upon request. Humana plans deny charges for services that lack appropriate order or referral documentation; when appropriate, plans require reimbursement of overpayments.

extracted_content.title: Claim Submission
extracted_content.hierarchy_path: Medicare Advantage Payment Policy > Claim Submission
extracted_content.content: A charge for a service that requires a valid order or referral must be submitted with the name and NPI of the ordering or referring provider, that provider must be a qualified healthcare provider, and that provider's name and NPI must be accurate and valid. Humana plans deny charges for services that require orders or referrals if those charges are not submitted as described herein; when appropriate, plans require reimbursement of overpayments.

reimbursement_guidelines.title: Reimbursement Guidelines
reimbursement_guidelines.content:
In addition to this policy, claims payments are subject to other plan requirements for the processing and payment of claims, including, but not limited to, requirements of medical necessity and reasonableness and applicable referral or authorization requirements.

Humana plans require valid orders for the same types of services for which Original Medicare requires orders and require valid referrals for the same types of services for which Original Medicare requires referrals. To be valid, an order or referral must have been issued by a qualified healthcare provider. The services of a Part A home health agency, specifically, may only be ordered or referred by a doctor of medicine, doctor of osteopathy or doctor of podiatry. Humana plans deny charges for services for which Humana requires valid orders or referrals when those services were provided in the absence of an applicable, valid order or referral; when appropriate, plans require reimbursement of overpayments.

Humana requires providers to maintain complete and accurate documentation of orders and referrals for services for which Humana requires orders and referrals. Humana requires providers to make order and referral documentation available to Humana upon request. Humana plans deny charges for services that lack appropriate order or referral documentation; when appropriate, plans require reimbursement of overpayments.

A charge for a service that requires a valid order or referral must be submitted with the name and NPI of the ordering or referring provider, that provider must be a qualified healthcare provider, and that provider's name and NPI must be accurate and valid. Humana plans deny charges for services that require orders or referrals if those charges are not submitted as described herein; when appropriate, plans require reimbursement of overpayments.

The following are examples of services that require ordering or referring provider information as described above. This is not an all- inclusive list.

Durable medical equipment, prosthetics, orthotics and supplies (DMEPOS)

Humana expects providers to follow the respective state Medicaid agency ordering and referring provider requirements. Humana Medicaid plans allow charges for services consistent with state Medicaid guidelines regarding ordering and referring provider requirements.

Applicable: An order or referral is applicable to rendered services when those services were provided pursuant to that order or referral.

Overpayments: Amounts paid to the provider for services that lack documentation.

Qualified healthcare provider: As used herein, means an individual licensed as one of the following: dental surgeon, doctor of medicine, doctor of osteopathy, doctor of dental medicine, doctor of podiatry, optometrist (may only order DME, laboratory and X-ray services), nurse practitioner, physician assistant, certified clinical nurse specialist, clinical psychologist, intern, resident, fellow, certified nurse midwife and clinical social worker.

Refer/referral: As used herein, means the process of a qualified healthcare provider directing work to another provider. This is also known as "certifying." It is thus distinct from the way that term might be used in any other contexts to describe the process established by the health plan to authorize outpatient specialty care services or inpatient services not rendered by the member's primary care physician.
